html:
The Lion Capital of Ashoka is the top of a stone column set up by the Maurya emperor Ashoka at Sarnath, near Varanasi, around 250 BCE. Sarnath is where the Buddha gave his first sermon.

Carved from a single block of sandstone and polished to a glassy shine, it shows four lions sitting back to back. Below them, on a round drum, run four wheels with 24 spokes alternating with a lion, an elephant, a bull and a horse. Beneath is an upturned bell-shaped lotus. A large stone wheel, the "wheel of dharma" that stands for the Buddha's teaching, once sat on the lions' heads.

The style shows links with the art of the Achaemenid Persian court, which also used polished stone and bell-shaped capitals.

The capital was found in excavations in 1905 and is in the Sarnath museum. In 1950 India adopted the four lions as its state emblem, and the wheel from the drum sits at the centre of the national flag. Other pillars carried the Edicts of Ashoka.
sum: The Lion Capital of Ashoka is the top of a stone column set up by the Maurya emperor Ashoka at Sarnath, near Varanasi, around 250 BCE. Sarnath is where the Buddha gave his first sermon.
